Transmission Media
      Anything that can carry information from source to
      its destination.

              Figure 7.1 Transmission medium and physical layer
Figure 7.2 Classes of transmission media

7-1 GUIDED MEDIA

 Guided media, which are those that provide a conduit
 from one device to another, include twisted-pair cable,
 coaxial cable, and fiber-optic cable.
      1. Twisted-Pair Cable
      2. Coaxial Cable
      3. Fiber-Optic Cable

Twisted-Pair Cable

  1) Least expensive, most widely used.

  2) Consists of two insulated copper wires arranged in a regular spiral pattern.

  3) Twisting tends to decrease crosstalk, interference between adjacent pairs in a cable.

  4) Tighter twisting provides much better performance but also increases cost.

  5) Separately insulated, twisted together.

  6) Often bundled into cables.

  Uses: I) Telephone lines. II) Usually installed in building daisy-chain construction.

Twisted-Pair Cable
      Twisted pair is categorized into two types:

      i)   Shielded Twisted-Pair (STP): STP has a metal foil or braided mesh covering that encases
           each pair of insulated conductors.
      ii)  Unshielded Twisted-Pair (UTP).

                              Figure 7.4 UTP and STP cables
Figure 7.5 UTP connector

Coaxial Cable
      i)     Coaxial cable (or coax) carries signals of higher frequency ranges.

      ii)    Consists of a hollow outer cylindrical conductor covered by a shield.

      iii)   Inner conductor is a solid metal, separated by insulating material; the whole cable is
             covered by a plastic cover.

      iv)    Due to its shielding, coaxial cables are much less susceptible to interference or
             crosstalk than twisted pair.

      Uses: LAN, television distribution, long-distance telephone cable.

                                       Figure 7.7 Coaxial cable

Optical Fiber

  The core consists of:

  1) Thin strands of fibers made of glass or plastic.

  2) The cladding is a glass or plastic coating that has optical properties different from those
     of the core.

  3) Thin, flexible medium, capable of guiding an optical ray.

  4) Made of ultra-pure fused silica, glass fiber, or even plastic.

  5) Small size and light weight.

  6) It has a cylindrical shape consisting of three concentric sections: core, cladding, and jacket
     (laser/LED is used as the light source).

  7) Uses: LAN, long-distance telecommunication.

Figure 7.11 Optical fiber

                              Figure 7.14 Fiber construction
Figure 7.10 Bending of light ray

Optical Fiber

  Advantages of Optical Fiber:

  1) Higher bandwidth.

  2) Less signal attenuation.

  3) Immunity to electromagnetic interference.

  4) Resistance to corrosive materials.

  Disadvantages of Optical Fiber:

  1) Installation and maintenance.

  2) Unidirectional light propagation.

  3) Cost.

Propagation Modes in Optical Fiber

Multimode: Refers to the variety of angles that will reflect. Multiple propagation
paths exist. Signal elements spread out in time and hence limit the data rate.
Single Mode: When the fiber core is reduced, fewer angles will reflect. By reducing the
radius of the core to the order of a wavelength, only a single angle (mode) can pass.

Propagation Modes in Optical Fiber

Multimode Step Index: The density of the core remains constant from center to edge. Step
index refers to the suddenness of the change, which contributes to the distortion of the signal as it
passes through the fiber.

In multimode step-index fiber, a beam of light moves through the constant-density core in a straight line
until it reaches the interface of the core and the cladding.

Multimode Graded Index:

1) Decreases distortion of the signal through the cable.

2) The density varies; it is highest at the center of the core and decreases gradually to its
   lowest at the edges.

3) By varying the refractive index of the core, rays may be focused more efficiently than in
   multimode step-index fiber.

7-2 UNGUIDED MEDIA: WIRELESS

   1. Unguided media transport electromagnetic waves without
      using a physical conductor.
   2. This type of communication is often referred to as wireless
      communication.
   3. Transmission and reception are by means of antennas.
      Carefully aligned antennas allow point-to-point
      communication.

Wireless Transmission Waves

Radio waves:
1) 3 kHz to 1 GHz.
2) Use omnidirectional (all-directional)
   antennas.
3) Used for multicast communications, such
   as AM/FM radio, television, marine
   radio, cordless phones, and paging
   systems.

                                      Figure 7.20 Omnidirectional antenna

Wireless Transmission Waves
Microwaves:
  1) 1 GHz to 300 GHz.
  2) Use unidirectional (sends signal in one direction only) antennas.
  3) Used for unicast communication such as cellular telephones, satellite
     networks, and wireless LANs.
Infrared signals:
   1) 300 GHz to 400 THz.
   2) Used for short-range communication in a closed area using line-of-
      sight propagation.
